clue.text: Heads out of place with Eraserhead's type of entry

parts.note: to place something is to set it down

indicators.note: entry means one piece goes into another, so the little word of enters the genre's two letters

parts.note: Eraserhead, David Lynch's 1977 film, is filed under SF, science fiction

explanation.surface: Something that seems out of place in a strange film like Lynch's Eraserhead.
explanation.walkthrough: The first 'of' is a link (definition of wordplay); the second 'of' is the letters that enter SF, signalled by 'entry'.
explanation.definitionFit: To set off is to start a journey, which is what someone who heads out does.

clue.text: Appear memorably as clue for "head-to-head"

parts.note: the head of a river is its spring or source
head also means mind, as in a good head for figures

explanation.surface: A clue writer explaining how the phrase head-to-head came to mind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'as clue for' is a link: each 'head' in 'head-to-head' is replaced by a synonym.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that springs to mind appears suddenly in one's memory or thoughts.

clue.text: See 1
Head out in car: to turn left, faced eight ways

indicators.note: in places the rearranged head inside the other rearrangement
turn says the letters of car and to are rearranged
out suggests disorder, so the letters of head are rearranged

explanation.surface: A driver heading out turns left in the car.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' makes AHED from HEAD; 'turn' makes OCTRA from CAR TO; 'in' puts AHED inside, giving OCTAHEDRA, then L.
explanation.definitionFit: An octahedral solid has eight faces, so it is faced eight ways.

clue.text: Head's expression of anger after very poor grade

indicators.note: after says the sound-alike piece follows the grade letter

parts.note: F is a fail grade in exams

indicators.note: expression of means voicing a word, so we hear a word for anger

parts.note: wrath is great anger, said in Britain to rhyme with moth

explanation.surface: A head teacher expresses anger at a pupil's dreadful grade.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Head' looks like a person in charge, but it is the froth on a glass of beer.
explanation.definitionFit: Froth is the foamy head on a poured beer.

clue.text: This land is in our heart and it's in the head

indicators.note: in the says the little word sits inside the organ that follows

parts.note: the brain is the organ in the head

explanation.surface: A patriotic declaration that the nation lives in our hearts and our heads.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe-s of 'it's' is a link meaning 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: The setter is British, so 'this land' is the country the clue is written in.

clue.text: Get dad drunk, say, involving a couple of parties

indicators.note: say tells us the phrase is spoken and heard as another word

parts.note: get is buy, dad is pa and drunk is tight, giving buy pa tight

explanation.surface: Getting dad drunk at a couple of parties.
explanation.walkthrough: BUY PA TIGHT, said quickly, sounds like the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Bipartite means having two parts or involving two parties, as a bipartite agreement does.

clue.text: When he was fated to die horribly: Julius' finale

indicators.note: horribly suggests something mangled, so the letters of die are rearranged
finale picks the final letter of Julius'

explanation.surface: Julius Caesar's fated death, his grim finale.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition reads with 'die' to make the sense: Caesar was fated to die on the Ides of March.
explanation.definitionFit: The Ides of March, 15 March, was the date Julius Caesar was warned of and murdered on.

clue.text: No limits to usable accommodation

indicators.note: accommodation suggests rearranging to fit, so the letters of to usable are reorganised

explanation.surface: A rule that there are no limits on using accommodation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'accommodation' looks like housing, but it is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Absolute means unrestricted, having no limits, as absolute power does.

clue.text: Ran back to railhead, headless chicken? Yes, precisely

indicators.note: back says the word ran is read in reverse
head picks the first letter of rail
headless says the first letter is cut from the synonym of chicken

parts.note: a chicken is a fowl

explanation.surface: A headless chicken running back to the railway station.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' makes NAR from RAN; 'headless' makes OWL from FOWL.
explanation.definitionFit: Narrowly can mean closely or precisely, as in narrowly defined.

clue.text: Mid-afternoon: lay back, stretch and relax

indicators.note: mid points to the central letter of the nine-letter word afternoon
lay back signals that the next word's synonym is read backwards

parts.note: a stretch is a period of time, as in a stretch in prison

explanation.surface: A lazy afternoon routine: lie back, stretch out and unwind.
explanation.definitionFit: To remit is an old sense meaning to slacken or ease off, as one does when relaxing.

clue.text: Persecutor of desperate poor owns the media

indicators.note: owns says the rearranged letters hold the media inside them
desperate suggests wild disorder, so the letters of poor are rearranged

parts.note: the press is the collective name for newspapers and journalists

explanation.surface: A claim that a media owner persecutes the desperate poor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'desperate' makes OPOR from POOR, which is split OP...OR around PRESS by 'owns'.
explanation.definitionFit: An oppressor is a tyrant who persecutes or keeps others down.

clue.text: Five-part harmonised note in most of the chorus: Boatman drops out before loud ending

indicators.note: most of means all but the last letter of the word the
drops out says the setter's pronoun leaves the synonym of chorus

parts.note: a chorus is a body of singers, a choir
the setter Boatman refers to himself as I

indicators.note: ending picks the last letter of loud

explanation.surface: A musical analysis of a five-voice chord, with the setter dropping out of the choir.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is adjectival in form but describes the chord: a five-note harmony.
explanation.definitionFit: A ninth chord stacks five notes (root, third, fifth, seventh, ninth), so it is harmony in five parts.

clue.text: Discovery of orchestral torch song performer

indicators.note: discovery of signals the answer is found lying inside the following words

explanation.surface: Finding a singer of torch songs in an orchestra.
explanation.definitionFit: An alto is a singer with a low female or high male voice in a choir.

clue.text: Cook flan and invert: fish course is ordered with it

definitions.text: fish course is ordered with it

indicators.note: cook means to doctor or alter, so the letters of flan and invert are rearranged

explanation.surface: A recipe: cook a flan and turn it out, with a fish course ordered alongside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fish course' looks like a menu item, but it means the route a fish swims, steered by this fin.
explanation.definitionFit: A ventral fin is on a fish's underside and helps it steer and keep its course steady.

clue.text: Tired out in the head? That's hurtful

indicators.note: out suggests something displaced, so the letters of tired are rearranged

parts.note: mental means relating to the mind, in the head

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether being tired is all in the mind, and is told that remark is hurtful.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' turns TIRED into DETRI.
explanation.definitionFit: Detrimental means harmful or damaging, close to hurtful.

clue.text: Head up onto river crossing in Kent

indicators.note: up in a down clue says the synonym of head is read from bottom to top

parts.note: nut is slang for head
a bridge carries a road over a river

explanation.surface: Climbing up onto a bridge over a river in Kent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'onto' is a link. TUNBRIDGE is the old spelling of Tonbridge, a Kent town, and part of Tunbridge Wells.
explanation.definitionFit: Tunbridge is a place name in the English county of Kent, a county in south-east England.

clue.text: Sign of distress in Spooner's dull head

indicators.note: Spooner's signals swapping the opening sounds of two words

parts.note: drear is a poetic word for dull or dreary
the top is the head of something

explanation.surface: Spooner, with a dull head, shows a sign of distress.
explanation.walkthrough: Swapping the opening sounds of DREAR TOP gives TEAR DROP.
explanation.definitionFit: A teardrop shed from the eye is a visible sign of sadness or upset.

clue.text: Showing no interest in getting much back, making no effort

indicators.note: back says the synonym of much is read in reverse

parts.note: lots means much, a great deal
to do something idly is to do it lazily, making no effort

explanation.surface: Someone who gets much back without effort shows no interest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' makes STOL from LOTS; 'interest' looks financial alongside 'getting much back', but it means curiosity.
explanation.definitionFit: Acting stolidly is acting impassively, without showing emotion or curiosity.

clue.text: Railhead activity leads to accident — rain mentioned in covering letters

indicators.note: the answer sits in a run of letters covered by the words that follow

explanation.surface: An account of a railway accident, with rain mentioned in letters of complaint.
explanation.walkthrough: 'leads to' is a link; the run starts at the end of accident.
explanation.definitionFit: Entraining is boarding a train, the activity at a railhead where troops or goods are loaded.

clue.text: Head takes in upper-class boisterousness

indicators.note: takes in says the slang word for head holds the class letter inside

parts.note: bonce is British slang for the head
U is the standard label for upper-class usage

explanation.surface: A head teacher allows some upper-class high spirits.
explanation.walkthrough: BONCE is everyday British slang for a person's head.
explanation.definitionFit: Bounce means liveliness or exuberant energy, which is boisterousness.

clue.text: High stakes: Sophie's head over heels

indicators.note: head picks the first letter of Sophie's

parts.note: a ship heels when it tilts or leans over

explanation.surface: Sophie falling head over heels at high-stakes gambling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'over' is a link here (the S goes over, on top of, TILTS in a down clue). 'High stakes' looks like gambling but means tall poles.
explanation.definitionFit: Stilts are tall poles, high stakes one walks on to stand above the ground.

clue.text: Headline?

parts.note: split into head (to govern) and line (to mark straight lines on paper): one word means both

explanation.surface: A one-word query about a newspaper heading.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'Headline' as two definitions run together: head, as in lead a country, and line, a ruled stroke.
explanation.definitionFit: To rule is to govern (head) and to draw lines with a straight edge, and a rule is a line.

clue.text: Clue to U-boat command?

parts.note: the answer read as wordplay says rearrange (order) the letters of U-boat, which gives about: so the answer is a clue to U-boat

explanation.surface: A naval hint about a submarine's command.
explanation.walkthrough: A reverse clue: the answer's first word is an anagram signal and its second is the anagram of U-BOAT.
explanation.definitionFit: To order someone about is to boss or command them around.

clue.text: Land of heartbreak?

indicators.note: break signals the letters of heart are smashed and reformed

explanation.surface: A country of heartbreak.
explanation.walkthrough: 'heartbreak' is one word, but 'break' acts on 'heart' within it.
explanation.definitionFit: Earth means land or ground, as well as the planet.

clue.text: It protects our heritage from worsening odds. Boatman supports it

definitions.text: It protects our heritage from worsening

indicators.note: supports in a down clue says the sailor sits under the odds

parts.note: SP, the starting price, is the odds offered when a horse race begins
Boatman is a sailor, an AB or able seaman

explanation.surface: A heritage society's warning about worsening odds, with the setter backing it.
explanation.walkthrough: SPAB is the Society for the Protection of Ancient Buildings, a British conservation charity.
explanation.definitionFit: The Society for the Protection of Ancient Buildings works to stop old buildings decaying.

clue.text: It damages the leaves of roses, leading to wounded pride

parts.note: reds are red roses, here a plural colour noun

indicators.note: wounded means hurt or damaged, so the letters of pride are rearranged

explanation.surface: A garden pest attacking rose leaves, to a gardener's wounded pride.
explanation.walkthrough: 'of' and 'leading to' are links; 'wounded' turns PRIDE into SPIDER.
explanation.definitionFit: The red spider mite is a tiny garden pest that feeds on and damages plant leaves.

clue.text: Last of its last in first: first of last?

indicators.note: its points back to the little word of, and last takes that word's closing letter

parts.note: A is first, as in an A grade or A1

indicators.note: first of takes the opening letter of the clue's closing word

explanation.surface: A riddling string of lasts and firsts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'its' points back to 'of', whose last letter gives F; the rest is a charade of IN, A and L.
explanation.definitionFit: Final means last, coming at the end.

clue.text: Outstanding leap by a player

indicators.note: a player plays with things, so the letters before it are rearranged

explanation.surface: A sporting moment: a leap by a player that stands out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Outstanding' looks like praise for the leap, but it is the definition, meaning owed.
explanation.definitionFit: An outstanding bill is still to be paid, so it is due for payment.

clue.text: After head start, wind up on winners' tail: put your shirt on them?

indicators.note: start points to the first letter of head

parts.note: to wind someone up is British slang for annoying them, rousing anger

indicators.note: tail points to the final letter of winners'

explanation.surface: A gambler's tip: back the winners and put your shirt on them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put your shirt on' sounds like betting everything, but here it is literal: shirts are put on clothes hangers.
explanation.definitionFit: Hangers are what you hang shirts on, a playful literal reading of a betting idiom.
